name: Liam Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a dragline at Coalbrook, an open-cut coal mine. A dragline's a digging machine the size of an apartment block. It swings a bucket on steel cables and strips the dirt off the top of the coal seam. I sit up in the house, that's the cab, with two levers and two pedals, and I swing and drag all shift. I like the rhythm of it. What I don't like is the nights, and the paperwork they keep adding.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been on the dragline?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nineteen years, same machine for the last eleven. The crew calls her Old Mary, because she's older than most of them. I'm not one for gadgets. My son Leo set up the phone so I can see the footy scores, and that's as far as I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that fuss for nothing. At work I'd have a laugh about it with the crew. I don't do anything online, so that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's what I expected. Nobody's putting a computer in charge of Old Mary. She's got moods, she's got quirks, you feel her through the seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working, keep paying the mortgage, keep the boat. Nadia and I would go on the same as we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, maybe, but mostly just normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you feel her through the seat. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the bucket catches rock instead of dirt, the whole machine shudders a certain way. You ease off before the cable snaps. Took me five years to learn that. I can't see a computer feeling it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone at work think differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young engineers, sure. They talk about the remote draglines at other mines. I let them talk. They've never had their tea spill when she swings.

S0.say: I'd say all that fuss came to nothing and have a laugh about it with the crew. I don't do anything online, so that would be the end of it.
S0.think: It's what I expected. Nobody's putting a computer in charge of Old Mary, because you feel her moods through the seat.
S0.do: Keeps working, keeps paying the mortgage and keeps the boat. Carries on family life with his partner exactly as before.
S0.feel: Calm and quietly pleased, mostly just normal.
S0.quote: They've never had their tea spill when she swings.
S0.fieldNote: Liam is completely settled in this picture and seems to have expected it. His confidence rests on feel and experience with one machine over eleven years. He mentions remote draglines elsewhere but files them under the young engineers' talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so let's see how it plays out. Some jobs will go, some won't. I'd say that at work, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think a dragline is near the bottom of the list. They'll do the trucks first, the dozers next. And Coalbrook's got maybe twelve years of coal left anyway, so I'm more worried about that than about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing for the first year. Watch what happens to the truck drivers. If it looks like it's coming for the draglines, then I'd think about it, but not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little bit of a nag in the back of the head, like a noise in the engine you decide to ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait and watch. What would make you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they put a remote dragline in at Coalbrook, that's the line. Or if the young engineers start sitting in the cab with laptops. I'd notice that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on your crew you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, the truck driver who brings my crew their lunch run. He's got three kids and he'd be first in line. I'd tell him to start looking, but I wouldn't take my own advice.

S1.say: I'd say it's coming, so let's see how it plays out, because some jobs will go and some won't. Nothing dramatic, just that at work.
S1.think: A dragline is near the bottom of the list, behind trucks and dozers. With maybe twelve years of coal left at Coalbrook, the mine closing worries me more than AI does.
S1.do: Does nothing different in the first year and watches what happens to the truck drivers. Says he'd only start thinking about options if a remote dragline arrived at his mine.
S1.feel: Calm, with a small nag he chooses to ignore, like a noise in the engine.
S1.quote: I'd tell him to start looking, but I wouldn't take my own advice.
S1.fieldNote: Liam's calm rests on a reasonable read that his machine is low on the list. He openly admits he'd give advice he wouldn't take, which is a candid picture of resistance. The mine's own lifespan matters more to him than technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is mad, and somebody should have stopped it. At work I'd be in the crib room with everyone else, trying to work out what it means. I'd ring my brother-in-law, because he always reads the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Old Mary gets a computer and I go home. If the AI can do anything, it can feel the bucket catch rock too. And my nineteen years count for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the boat the first month and cut everything that isn't the house and the kids. We'd put every spare cent on the mortgage. I'd talk to Nadia's brother, who has a landscaping business, about whether there'd be work there, though I suppose robots would do that too. Beyond that I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground giving way under the machine, which is the one thing we're trained to fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. Would you try anything new in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't know where to start. I'd be the bloke at the back of a computer class not understanding a word. I'd rather save money than waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo and Ava?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo's thirteen, he'd want the facts. I'd tell him we'll be fine, we've got savings. Ava's eight, she'd just want to know if we can still go to the lake.

S2.say: I'd say this is mad and somebody should have stopped it. I'd be in the crib room trying to work out what it means and ringing my brother-in-law, who follows the news.
S2.think: Old Mary gets a computer and I go home. If AI can do anything, it can feel the bucket catch rock too, and my nineteen years count for nothing.
S2.do: Sells the boat in the first month and cuts all spending beyond the house and the kids. Puts every spare cent on the mortgage and asks his brother-in-law about work in his landscaping business.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the ground giving way under the machine.
S2.quote: Like the ground giving way under the machine, which is the one thing we're trained to fear.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI is the first picture to break Liam's faith in the feel of the job. He reaches for cuts and family rather than retraining, which he dismisses quickly. His reach out to his brother-in-law is tentative, and he spots himself that robots might do that work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, but at least there's some warning. I'd talk about it at work, more than I'd want to. I'd probably listen more than talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd be forty-eight. Coalbrook would probably still be open, but they'd put a remote system on Old Mary. I'd maybe have three years before it bites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save harder, putting the overtime straight on the mortgage. I'd sell the boat in year two or three, not right away. And I'd wait and see what the company offers, because they'd have to offer something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be doing more sums than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned waiting to see what the company offers. What if they offer retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at it. I'm not saying no. But I'd want to know it leads to an actual job at the end. I've seen courses that lead nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, what does five years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can pay off most of the mortgage. Two, I'm scrambling. It's the difference between a soft landing and a hard one.

S3.say: I'd say it's too fast, but at least there's some warning. I'd talk about it at work more than I'd like, though mostly I'd listen.
S3.think: I'd be 48, Coalbrook would still be open, and they'd fit a remote system to Old Mary. I'd probably have three years before it bites.
S3.do: Keeps working and puts overtime straight onto the mortgage, selling the boat in the second or third year. Waits to see what retraining or help the company offers before deciding anything.
S3.feel: Anxious and doing more sums than he'd like.
S3.quote: It's the difference between a soft landing and a hard one.
S3.fieldNote: Five years softens Liam's reaction, mainly because it lets him nearly clear the mortgage. He still waits on the company to make the first move, a pattern across every scenario. He's more open to retraining here than earlier, but only if it clearly leads to a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of warning, and the companies and government should use it. I'd say that at work, though I'd add that nobody really knows what'll happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is different. I'd be fifty-three, the house would be paid off, the kids nearly grown. Coalbrook might close by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving like now. Leo's talking about doing a mining apprenticeship, and I'd have a word with him about that. Maybe something like plumbing, where people still want a person in their house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly about the kids, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leo about plumbing instead of mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, son, I'm proud of what I do, but times change. Find something where people need you in the room. He'd probably argue, he's stubborn like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything about your own work in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much, if I'm honest. I'd ride Old Mary till they take her away. I've got the savings to sit tight, and I'm not a man for big changes.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning and companies and government should use it. I'd add that nobody really knows what will happen.
S4.think: Ten years is different: at 53 the house is paid off and the kids nearly grown. Coalbrook might close by then anyway.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving as he does now. Talks his son out of a mining apprenticeship and towards a trade like plumbing.
S4.feel: Uneasy, mostly about the kids rather than himself.
S4.quote: I'd ride Old Mary till they take her away.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Liam settles into riding out his career on the machine he knows. His real concern moves to Leo's choices, where he shows more flexibility than he applies to himself. He admits plainly that he's not a man for big changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time to get ready. What would help is a decent payout from the company, a year's pay at least, and some time to work out what to do next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. If Coalbrook goes, the whole town goes: the pub, the footy club, the shops. That's what keeps me up, more than my own job.

headlineQuote: If Coalbrook goes, the whole town goes: the pub, the footy club, the shops.
portrait: Liam Costa is 43 and has run a dragline at Coalbrook open-cut coal mine for nineteen years, the last eleven on the same machine, Old Mary. He trusts feel and experience over gadgets and never uses AI tools. Savings and a half-paid house keep him calm through the gentler scenarios, where he expects his machine to be low on the automation list. Fast AGI alarms him, and he responds with cuts rather than retraining; with more warning he simply plans to ride out his career and steer his son towards a trade.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there would be no time to get ready.
whatWouldHelp: A decent company payout of at least a year's pay, plus time to work out what to do next.
